articles.title: Nikesh Arora Is Buying the Whole Security Stack. The Bill Is Already Past $28 Billion.
articles.excerpt: Palo Alto Networks just closed its $3.3 billion Chronosphere deal weeks after swallowing CyberArk for $25 billion. For the Indians who fill its engineering ranks, the consolidation is the career.
articles.image_caption: Palo Alto Networks chairman and CEO Nikesh Arora speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt
articles.nri_angle: Palo Alto Networks, run by Indian-origin CEO Nikesh Arora, is consolidating the cybersecurity industry around AI agents — reshaping the job market for the thousands of Indian engineers who staff security teams in Santa Clara, Bengaluru and beyond.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Qualcomm Is Reportedly Spending $10 Billion to Finally Crash Nvidia's Party
articles.excerpt: The Snapdragon maker is in talks to buy AI-chip startup Tenstorrent days before an investor day where it will lay out a data-centre plan. For the Indian engineers who power Qualcomm, the pivot is personal.
articles.image_caption: Close-up of a computer circuit board showing electronic components
articles.nri_angle: Qualcomm employs thousands of Indian engineers across Hyderabad, Bengaluru and San Diego; its bet to leap from phone chips into AI data-centre silicon decides what those engineers build next — and whether India's chip-design talent gets a seat at the AI hardware table.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Chip Bet Has a Quiet Winner: A Bengaluru Startup Making the 'Power Brain' for AI Data Centres
articles.excerpt: Peak XV just led a $15 million round into C2i, which builds the power-delivery silicon that keeps GPUs alive. It is the part of India's semiconductor story that doesn't need a billion-dollar fab.
articles.image_caption: Macro shot of a circuit board highlighting electronic components
articles.nri_angle: India's semiconductor mission is mostly about design IP, not fabs — and design-led startups like C2i are where NRI investors and returning engineers can actually get exposure to the chip story without waiting a decade for a factory.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Tech's 2026 Layoffs Just Passed 183,000. For Indians on H-1B, the Real Clock Is 60 Days.
articles.excerpt: The cuts aren't a recession — they're an AI restructuring. And no group is more exposed to the fallout than Indian visa holders.
articles.image_caption: Silicon Valley, epicentre of the 2026 tech layoff wave now topping 183,000 jobs (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indians hold the largest share of H-1B visas, and a layoff triggers a brutal 60-day deadline to find a new sponsor or leave the US — making the 2026 AI-driven cuts an existential threat, not just a career setback.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Switched On UPI in a Nice Department Store. It's Now in Nine Countries — and That's the Point.
articles.excerpt: India's homegrown payment rail is becoming an export of soft power. For NRIs, it's both a travel perk and a tell on where Indian fintech is headed.
articles.image_caption: UPI payments are now accepted in nine countries (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: UPI's overseas rollout means NRIs can soon pay abroad with their home apps — but it's also a leading indicator for Indian fintech firms like Razorpay and PhonePe now lining up IPOs that diaspora investors can access.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: One in Five ChatGPT Users Is Now Indian. OpenAI Just Told the World Where Its Future Is.
articles.excerpt: India makes up 20% of ChatGPT's billion users — and OpenAI is pouring data centers and Tata partnerships into the market. The diaspora sits on both sides of the trade.
articles.image_caption: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has called India the company's fastest-growing market
articles.nri_angle: India is becoming OpenAI's largest market, drawing data-center investment and enterprise deals that make it a serious place to build — even as the same AI boom threatens the IT-services jobs that employ much of the diaspora's network.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Minted Its First Space Unicorn. The Money Came From Singapore, BlackRock — and the Founders of Swiggy.
articles.excerpt: Skyroot's $60 million round crowns a Hyderabad rocket startup at a $1.1 billion valuation. For NRIs who grew up watching ISRO from the sidelines, private Indian space is now an asset class.
articles.image_caption: India's booming private space sector has produced its first unicorn (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: India's first billion-dollar private space company gives NRI investors and engineers a credible on-ramp into a deep-tech sector that was, until five years ago, entirely closed to anyone outside the government.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: TCS Just Opened India's First Oracle AI Lab. The Company That Sold Cheap Labor Is Trying to Sell Intelligence Instead.
articles.excerpt: A new Kolkata center, with four more planned, signals how India's biggest IT firm wants to survive an AI shift that is gutting its old headcount-driven model — the one that put millions of Indians on H-1B visas.
articles.image_caption: Tata Consultancy Services, which has opened India's first Oracle AI lab (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The pyramid model that staffed thousands of Indian engineers onto H-1B and L-1 visas is being hollowed out by AI; TCS's pivot to AI 'centers of excellence' shows what the diaspora's oldest career ladder is mutating into.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A US Cybersecurity Firm Just Opened in Bengaluru and Said the Quiet Part Out Loud: It Came for the Talent, Not the Discount.
articles.excerpt: N-able's new India center, and a GCC workforce headed toward 2.36 million, mark a turning point — global firms now build core tech in India because of who is there, not because it is cheap.
articles.image_caption: University of Michigan's Ford School via flickr (BY-ND)
articles.nri_angle: As US firms move core engineering — not just support — into India captive centers for the talent, the calculus for NRIs weighing a return home shifts: the best jobs are no longer only in Silicon Valley.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Vinod Khosla Says India's $200 Billion IT Industry 'Will Be Gone.' The Diaspora's Oldest Career Ladder Is Wobbling.
articles.excerpt: The Silicon Valley investor's warning landed the same week Accenture cratered and Infosys and Wipro shares tumbled — and it hits the exact path many NRIs took to America.
articles.image_caption: Vinod Khosla, Sun Microsystems co-founder and venture capitalist, speaking at SXSW in 2024.
articles.nri_angle: The TCS-to-H-1B-to-green-card pipeline was the classic NRI on-ramp to America; Khosla's warning that AI agents will gut Indian IT threatens both the careers of family back home and the portfolios of diaspora investors betting on Indian tech.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Tesla Opened Its Fifth India Showroom in a Tech Hub Full of Future NRIs. The Price Tag Tells You Who It's Really For.
articles.excerpt: The new Hyderabad Experience Center sells a Model Y for around $61,000 — far above its US price — as Tesla tests Indian demand without yet building a factory.
articles.image_caption: A Tesla Model Y; the company opened its fifth India showroom as it courts affluent urban buyers
articles.nri_angle: NRIs who bought a Model Y in California for under $50,000 are now watching family in Hyderabad get quoted $61,000-plus for the same car — a vivid example of import-duty arbitrage and a live issue in US-India trade talks Tesla investors are tracking.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Will Build a Quarter of the World's iPhones This Year. A Pollution Notice Shows How Hard the Climb Still Is.
articles.excerpt: Apple's bet to diversify out of China is working — but a Tata factory notice, recalled Foxconn engineers and a steep supplier learning curve reveal the growing pains behind the headline.
articles.image_caption: Nick Kenrick.. via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: Apple's Tamil Nadu and Karnataka plants are reshaping the hometown economies of millions of NRIs' families, turning the 'India rising' story into tangible skilled-manufacturing jobs — and a live bet for diaspora investors on whether India moves beyond final assembly.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ambani Just Priced India's Biggest IPO Ever. Two American Tech Giants Are Already Inside Jio.
articles.excerpt: Reliance filed Jio Platforms' draft prospectus Friday, targeting a record $3.8 billion — and NRIs holding any S&P 500 fund already own a sliver of it through Meta and Google.
articles.image_caption: Mukesh Ambani, whose Reliance has priced India's biggest-ever IPO for Jio
articles.nri_angle: Jio's record IPO is the cleanest direct route yet for NRIs to own India's largest digital business — but it arrives in a soft Sensex with rupee and timing risk to weigh.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Canadian Pension Fund Just Bet $1 Billion on India's AI Plumbing. The Diaspora Builds Both Ends of It.
articles.excerpt: CPP Investments is backing Hyderabad's CtrlS Datacenters to scale tenfold — a sign global capital sees India's AI demand as real, not speculative.
articles.image_caption: calix via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: India's AI infrastructure is being financed by global pension capital and built by Indian operators, with much of the cloud engineering routed through NRI-heavy teams in Hyderabad and Bengaluru.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: BigBasket Just Hired an Amazon Veteran to Save It. The Company That Invented Indian Grocery Is Now the Underdog.
articles.excerpt: Tata handed the CEO job to ex-Amazon executive Amit Nanda as losses widened 46% and 10-minute rivals Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart pulled ahead.
articles.image_caption: Packed grocery delivery orders ready for dispatch, as India's quick-commerce race intensifies
articles.nri_angle: BigBasket is the pipeline many NRIs use to supply aging parents in India, so a leadership shake-up amid the quick-commerce squeeze is a daily-life signal as much as an investing one.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Google Put Gemini in a $99 Speaker. The Real Target Is the Phone in Every Indian Pocket.
articles.excerpt: Sundar Pichai is smuggling his AI into the devices people already own — and India is the test bed, not the afterthought.
articles.image_caption: Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, who is steering the company's Gemini-everywhere strategy.
articles.nri_angle: Indian Americans sit on both sides of this launch — as the engineers inside Alphabet whose teams live or die by Gemini, and as NRIs whose families in India are Google's first test market for its AI-everywhere strategy.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nvidia's Biggest Threat Isn't a Rival. It's the Customers Now Selling Their Own Chips.
articles.excerpt: Amazon and Google are pushing custom AI silicon into the open market — and Indian engineers are building hardware on every side of the fight.
articles.image_caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang; the chipmaker's biggest customers are now designing their own AI silicon (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin engineers staff the silicon, memory, networking, and security layers of the AI stack at once, so the breakup of Nvidia's monopoly directly shapes diaspora careers and NRI investment portfolios.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Satya Nadella Warned Against AI Monopolies. Days Later He Started Charging by the Task.
articles.excerpt: Microsoft's new usage-based Copilot agents reveal where the most valuable work is heading — and what it means for the Indians who do so much of it.
articles.image_caption: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, who is reshaping Copilot around autonomous, usage-billed AI agents.
articles.nri_angle: Microsoft's pivot to billing for autonomous AI work hits the structured, multi-step knowledge tasks that Indian engineers and IT-services firms built their economic model on, redrawing which careers survive.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Accenture's Stock Just Cratered to a 7-Year Low. The Company That Employs the Most Indians Is Flashing a Warning.
articles.excerpt: Bookings shrank, AI clients are stalling at the pilot stage, and the firm has stopped breaking out its AI revenue. For Indian engineers, the world's biggest consultancy is the canary in the coal mine.
articles.image_caption: Accenture chair and CEO Julie Sweet speaking at the World Economic Forum
articles.nri_angle: Accenture employs more Indians than any other firm on earth; its stalling bookings and AI-driven caution are an early signal for the hundreds of thousands of Indian engineers whose careers run through global IT services.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An American Manufacturer Is Teaming With Adani to Build India's AI Backbone. The Diaspora Should Watch Where the Racks Get Made.
articles.excerpt: Jabil and the Adani Group plan a vertically integrated factory for AI data-center hardware in India — racks, cooling, power — chasing a market they peg at over $3 trillion. It is the unglamorous half of the AI boom, and India wants it.
articles.image_caption: The Rick Smith Show via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs weighing whether India can move up the AI value chain beyond software services, a US-India factory making the physical hardware of data centers is the most concrete test yet of the 'build it at home' thesis.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: DeepSeek Just Raised $7.4 Billion to Stay Chinese. India's AI Startups Are Watching the Playbook Closely.
articles.excerpt: The lab that rattled Silicon Valley took outside money for the first time — through a structure designed so its founder never loses control. For India's sovereign-AI push and the diaspora that funds it, it is a lesson in how to scale without selling out.
articles.image_caption: Jwz1000520 via wikimedia (CC0)
articles.nri_angle: DeepSeek's founder-control funding model is a template India's own AI champions — and the NRI investors backing them — are studying as they try to build sovereign AI without ceding control to foreign capital.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Men Who Run Microsoft and Google Just Bought a Piece of Lord's. The Buyer's List Reads Like an NRI Yearbook.
articles.excerpt: A consortium led by Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora — with Satya Nadella, Sundar Pichai and Shantanu Narayen — paid roughly £195 million for 49% of London Spirit, outbidding an IPL billionaire.
articles.image_caption: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, who led the consortium that bought a 49% stake in London Spirit.
articles.nri_angle: Four of the most powerful Indian-origin executives in global tech just turned their personal wealth toward cricket at Lord's — a vivid sign of where diaspora capital and cultural identity are converging.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Adobe Is Giving Its AI Away for Free. Shantanu Narayen Is Betting the Crowd Comes Back to Pay.
articles.excerpt: On its Q2 call, Adobe paused Creative Cloud price hikes and pushed free versions of its AI tools — freemium users jumped to 90 million — and raised full-year guidance even as the strategy squeezes near-term revenue.
articles.image_caption: Adobe chairman and CEO Shantanu Narayen, who is steering the company through its AI transition.
articles.nri_angle: Adobe under Indian-origin CEO Shantanu Narayen is a core holding for many NRI investors and a major employer of Indian engineers — its bet to give AI away and chase scale over margin is a wager the whole diaspora-heavy software sector is now making.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Razorpay Just Filed Quietly for Its IPO. India's Payment Giants Are Lining Up to Cash Out — and NRIs Want In.
articles.excerpt: The Bengaluru fintech confidentially submitted its draft prospectus to SEBI as UPI volumes hit record highs, joining a 2026 pipeline that already includes the NSE and a wave of consumer-tech listings.
articles.image_caption: The Razorpay logo; the payments giant has filed confidentially for an IPO as India's fintech leaders line up to go public
articles.nri_angle: A generation of Indian fintech unicorns NRIs read about for years is finally heading to public markets — turning private bets into something diaspora investors can actually own, if they understand the cross-border rules.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian IT Giant Just Bought Into the AI That Could Replace It. The Logic Is Colder Than It Looks.
articles.excerpt: HCLTech's $150 million bet on Sarvam AI is the first time an Indian services firm has taken a real stake in a homegrown model-maker. It is less a vote of confidence than a hedge.
articles.image_caption: HCLTech chief executive C Vijayakumar, who is steering the company into sovereign AI.
articles.nri_angle: For the hundreds of thousands of Indians whose careers run through TCS, Infosys, Wipro and HCL — on H-1Bs in New Jersey or in Bengaluru delivery centers — this deal signals which skills the services industry will pay for next, and which it is quietly writing off.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Threads Just Hit 500 Million Users. The Quiet Engine Behind It Is India.
articles.excerpt: Meta's three-year-old text app is now the size of X — and much of its organic, sticky growth is coming from the creators, fandoms and diaspora arguments that flourish in the Indian internet.
articles.image_caption: The Threads logo; Meta's text-based app crossed 500 million monthly users, with India among its fastest-growing markets
articles.nri_angle: Threads has become the default room where Indian creators, cricket fandoms and NRI commentators argue in real time — so where Meta steers the app next directly shapes how the diaspora talks to itself, and how brands reach it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ghar Wapsi: India's Startups Are Sprinting Home Before They IPO. NRI Investors Should Read the Fine Print.
articles.excerpt: Meesho, Zepto, Pine Labs and now Pocket FM are unwinding their offshore holding companies to list in Mumbai. The 'reverse flip' is reshaping who gets to own India's next public tech.
articles.image_caption: Wikimedia Commons (CC)
articles.nri_angle: When a startup moves its parent from Delaware or Singapore back to India ahead of an IPO, the listing happens on Indian exchanges — changing exactly how, and whether, an NRI in the US can buy in, and what tax bill comes with it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ola Electric Was Supposed to Win India's EV Race. It Just Lost Half Its Market in a Year.
articles.excerpt: TVS, Bajaj and a quietly relentless Ather have overtaken the one-time disruptor — and diaspora investors are learning that share price and market share have decoupled.
articles.image_caption: Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (CC)
articles.nri_angle: Three of India's top EV two-wheeler makers are publicly listed, and NRIs investing through GIFT City and family demat accounts are watching a market where execution, not hype, now decides the winners.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Deep-Tech Pitch Just Raised $254 Million — in France. For the Diaspora, It's an Invitation.
articles.excerpt: Bharat Innovates 2026 channelled capital into space, chips and AI, and launched cross-border funds aimed squarely at NRIs who have watched India's tech wealth from the sidelines.
articles.image_caption: A founder pitches at a tech conference, evoking the startup-investor sessions at Bharat Innovates 2026
articles.nri_angle: New cross-border funds unveiled at the summit are designed to let diaspora investors and returning engineers buy into India's hard-tech frontier — space, semiconductors, AI — for the first time at the early stage.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Jensen Huang Says the AI Era's Top Customer Isn't Human. India's Coders Should Listen Closely.
articles.excerpt: At Computex, NVIDIA pitched a future built for software agents, not people — and the work India has exported for thirty years is exactly what those agents replace first.
articles.image_caption: NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang, who used Computex 2026 to argue AI agents are computing's new primary customer
articles.nri_angle: Indian engineers fill NVIDIA's software stack, the hyperscaler AI teams, and the IT-services giants whose billable-human-hours model is precisely what agentic computing threatens to automate away.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Trump Says Apple Will Build Chips With Intel. The Fine Print Is Thinner Than the Headline.
articles.excerpt: A Truth Social post sent Intel's stock to a record and revived the dream of American-made silicon. For the Indian engineers who design Apple's chips, the question is what "made in America" actually changes.
articles.image_caption: Close-up of a computer processor, the kind of advanced silicon at the center of the Apple-Intel manufacturing talks
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin engineers fill Apple's silicon teams and Intel's foundry ranks, so a US chip-reshoring push reshapes the career map for the diaspora working at the heart of America's semiconductor revival.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Chip Dream Has a Quieter Second Act: Packaging the World's Silicon
articles.excerpt: While the headlines chase Tata's $11 billion fab, a Bengaluru company is selling India as the back-end of the global chip industry — and Japan is buying. It may be the more realistic bet.
articles.image_caption: A patterned silicon wafer, the raw output that semiconductor assembly and test firms cut, package and verify into finished chips
articles.nri_angle: Semiconductor packaging and test is the layer of India's chip ambition most likely to create jobs and exports first, giving diaspora professionals in the field a credible reason to weigh a move home or an investment in the sector.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Micron Reports Earnings Tuesday With Its Stock Up 245%. An Indian-American CEO Is Riding the AI Memory Boom.
articles.excerpt: Sanjay Mehrotra's company has sold out its entire 2026 supply of the memory chips that feed AI. For NRI investors, the rally is intoxicating — and the warning signs are flashing.
articles.image_caption: Sanjay Mehrotra, the Indian-American chief executive of Micron Technology
articles.nri_angle: Micron is led by an Indian-American CEO, is building a major plant in Gujarat, and has become one of the most widely held AI plays among NRI investors — making its earnings a personal event for the diaspora's portfolios.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Cognizant Just Wired ServiceNow's AI Agents Into Its Own. The Company That Sells Indian Labor Is Selling Orchestration Now.
articles.excerpt: The IT-services giant that employs hundreds of thousands of Indians is repositioning as the conductor of enterprise AI agents — a pivot that decides whether the diaspora's career ladder survives automation.
articles.image_caption: Cognizant's delivery center in Bangalore, one of the company's large Indian engineering hubs
articles.nri_angle: Cognizant employs more Indians than almost any US-listed firm; its bet that the future is orchestrating AI agents rather than writing code signals which skills will keep H-1B careers alive — and which won't.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: ISRO Is Betting Its Reputation on One Rocket Launch in Early July. After Two Failures, the Diaspora Is Watching Its Money Too.
articles.excerpt: India's workhorse PSLV returns to the pad after back-to-back failures grounded a rocket that private startups and foreign clients depend on — and a new generation of NRI-backed space firms is riding on the comeback.
articles.image_caption: An ISRO PSLV rocket lifts off from Sriharikota carrying the CMS-01 satellite
articles.nri_angle: India's space program has become an investable sector, not just a source of pride; whether ISRO restores the PSLV's credibility shapes the bet NRI capital is making on Skyroot, Agnikul, and a privatized launch market.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Real AI War Isn't About Chatbots. It's About Who Owns the Data Underneath — and Indian Engineers Are Building Both Sides.
articles.excerpt: Snowflake, Databricks, Microsoft and the model makers are converging on a single fight over the enterprise 'system of intelligence' — the layer that decides whose AI agents actually get to run a company.
articles.image_caption: exit78 via flickr (CC0)
articles.nri_angle: Indian data engineers staff the platform teams at Snowflake, Databricks, and every cloud fighting this war; the winner of the enterprise data-and-agent battle determines which skills — SQL warehousing or ML pipelines — keep diaspora careers in demand.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's First Insurtech IPO of 2026 Opens Friday. The Grey Market Is Telling Investors to Slow Down.
articles.excerpt: Turtlemint wants ₹883 crore to chase insurance in India's small towns. NRIs hunting the next fintech listing should read the muted premium before the hype.
articles.image_caption: The Bombay Stock Exchange in Mumbai, where Turtlemint shares are set to list on June 29 (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRIs who treat Indian fintech IPOs as a way to keep money working back home need to weigh Turtlemint's still-unprofitable model and flat grey-market premium before subscribing through their GIFT City or NRE-linked demat accounts.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An IIT Just Open-Sourced an AI That Thinks in 22 Indian Languages. It Could Outlast the Billion-Dollar Startups.
articles.excerpt: While Sarvam raises unicorn rounds, IIT Bombay's BharatGen is quietly building sovereign AI as public infrastructure — and the diaspora's engineers may matter more here than its investors.
articles.image_caption: Kuber Patel, Rosehub via wikimedia (BY-SA)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin AI researchers abroad, who often feel locked out of building for their mother tongues at Western labs, now have an open, government-backed platform to contribute to — and NRI parents get AI that actually understands the languages their kids are losing.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: At the G7's AI Table, Seven Companies Got a Seat. Only One Was Indian — and It's a Two-Year-Old Startup.
articles.excerpt: Sarvam's Pratyush Kumar sat beside Sam Altman and Demis Hassabis at Evian. For the diaspora, the symbolism is bigger than the startup.
articles.image_caption: World leaders at a recent G7 summit; Sarvam AI was the only Indian firm invited to the summit's AI working session (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: After a decade of Indian-origin executives running other countries' tech giants, a homegrown Indian AI company sitting at the G7 table marks a shift the diaspora has waited for — from running the West's companies to representing India's own.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nikesh Arora Just Closed His Third Big Deal in a Year. He's Betting $30 Billion That AI Will Break Security as We Know It.
articles.excerpt: Palo Alto Networks completed its $3.35 billion buy of Chronosphere — the latest in a buying spree by the Indian American CEO who keeps putting his own money on the line.
articles.image_caption: Palo Alto Networks Chairman and CEO Nikesh Arora speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt
articles.nri_angle: Palo Alto Networks is a major Bay Area employer of Indian engineers, and its Indian American CEO's aggressive AI-security strategy is a leading indicator for thousands of diaspora careers and portfolios.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Opendoor Is Shutting Its Entire India Operation. The Reason Isn't Cost — It's That AI Made the Work Disappear.
articles.excerpt: The real-estate platform is winding down its Chennai and Bengaluru offices, affecting 250 employees, and says the back-office work simply no longer needs to exist offshore.
articles.image_caption: Bengaluru's tech corridor; Opendoor is shutting its India engineering operation as AI absorbs the work (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The wage-arbitrage offshoring model that built India's tech industry and funded a generation of NRI migration faces its first AI-driven existential test — reshaping the pipeline that brought the diaspora to America.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Washington Just Barred 'Foreign Nationals' From Anthropic's Best AI — Including the Indian Engineers Who Built It.
articles.excerpt: A first-of-its-kind US export order forced Anthropic to pull Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 offline worldwide, drawing a line straight through the diaspora's professional life.
articles.image_caption: Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI models at the center of new US export limits (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: A huge share of frontier-AI-lab researchers are Indian nationals on visas — and a US order barring 'foreign nationals' from the top models puts the diaspora's dual identity at the center of a sovereignty fight.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Wipro Built a Whole Center to Run Claude. The Company That Sold Cheap Code Is Now Selling AI to Replace It.
articles.excerpt: The Bengaluru IT giant will certify 10,000 staff on Anthropic's models in 18 months — a defensive pivot that quietly redraws the career math for every Indian engineer who came up through the services pipeline.
articles.image_caption: Wipro's campus in Bengaluru; the IT giant is retraining staff around Anthropic's Claude models (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: For the hundreds of thousands of Indian engineers — and their relatives in the US and UK — who climbed out of the IT services pipeline that Wipro built, the company's bet on Claude is a signal that the old ladder of 'learn to code, get placed, get an H-1B' is being rebuilt around AI fluency rather than headcount.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's First Real Chip Fab Just Signed the Hardest Vendor in Tech. Now the Hard Part Begins.
articles.excerpt: Tata Electronics has locked in ASML lithography for its $11 billion Dholera fab, with first chips due by December — a milestone that turns India's semiconductor talk into a delivery deadline.
articles.image_caption: ASML, the Dutch lithography monopoly, will supply the equipment for Tata's Dholera chip fab in Gujarat (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin semiconductor engineers staff the design and process teams at Micron, Intel, AMD, Applied Materials and ASML's own customers — and a working fab in Gujarat is the first credible reason in a generation for some of them to consider building chips at home instead of abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Biggest Exchange Finally Filed to Go Public. At $57 Billion, NRIs Are About to Get a Piece of the Casino's House.
articles.excerpt: After years of regulatory delay, the National Stock Exchange filed IPO papers this week — a once-blocked listing that hands a $2.6 billion windfall to early backers and a rare shot at owning the rails of India's markets.
articles.image_caption: The National Stock Exchange of India in Mumbai, which has filed for a long-awaited IPO (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRIs have spent years pouring money into Indian stocks through the NSE's platform; its long-delayed IPO is the first realistic chance for diaspora investors — increasingly able to buy in via GIFT City and global brokerages — to own the exchange itself rather than just trade on it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Qualcomm Is Betting $10 Billion That the Phone Era Is Over. The Data Center Is the New Battleground.
articles.excerpt: The chipmaker is in talks to buy Tenstorrent and its star engineer Jim Keller, days before an investor day meant to convince Wall Street it can challenge Nvidia. For the Indian engineers who staff its chip-design ranks, it's a whole new product line.
articles.image_caption: Qualcomm President and CEO Cristiano Amon, who is steering the company toward data-center and edge-AI silicon
articles.nri_angle: Qualcomm employs thousands of Indian-origin chip engineers in the US and runs huge design centers in Bengaluru and Hyderabad; a pivot into data-center AI silicon reshapes the careers and job map for that workforce.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sriram Krishnan Is Leaving the White House AI Job. The Diaspora Got a Seat at the Table — and a Lesson in Its Limits.
articles.excerpt: The most senior Indian-American voice on AI policy exits at the end of June, just as Washington restricts foreign access to frontier models and revives a $100,000 H-1B fee. Representation, it turns out, isn't the same as protection.
articles.image_caption: Sriram Krishnan, the outgoing Senior White House Policy Advisor on Artificial Intelligence
articles.nri_angle: An Indian-American held the top AI policy seat in the White House, but the administration's H-1B fee and foreign-national model restrictions hit Indian tech workers hardest — a pointed lesson on the gap between having representation and having protection.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: You Can Now Pay With UPI at a Department Store in Nice. India's Payment Rail Is Quietly Going Global.
articles.excerpt: Within weeks, UPI has gone live in France and Cambodia, pushing past eight countries for merchant payments. For the diaspora, the real prize isn't tourist convenience — it's faster, cheaper remittances.
articles.image_caption: India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI), the real-time payment rail now expanding to overseas merchants
articles.nri_angle: UPI's overseas rollout means NRIs get a familiar payment app abroad and, more importantly, cheaper instant cross-border remittances that threaten the fees of legacy money-transfer operators.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Tim Cook Says Your Next iPhone Costs More. Blame the AI Memory Crunch — and Thank an Indian CEO for It.
articles.excerpt: The same shortage driving Apple's price hikes is minting profits for Micron's Sanjay Mehrotra. The diaspora sits on both sides of the trade.
articles.image_caption: Micron Technology chairman, president and CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, the Indian-origin chip executive whose memory business is benefiting from the AI-driven shortage
articles.nri_angle: Indian American households buy a lot of Apple gear and will feel the price hikes, while the global memory crunch driving them is enriching Micron's Indian-origin CEO Sanjay Mehrotra and pulling India deeper into the chip supply chain.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Funded an AI That Watches the Country From Orbit. For the Diaspora, It's a New Kind of Homecoming.
articles.excerpt: A $2.6 million grant to Bengaluru's SatSure signals India's push for sovereign Earth-observation AI — and a first real career pitch to diaspora space scientists.
articles.image_caption: An earth-observation satellite; India is funding AI to monitor the country from orbit
articles.nri_angle: A large share of the global space and geospatial workforce is Indian; India's private space push and its bet on sovereign Earth-observation AI is the first credible come-home-or-invest pitch in their own field.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
